findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: PPP contract obligations increasing; prior five-year saving of £4.5 million from 2023 plan is being reversed with £1 million per annum added from year 3 onwards.
findings.detail: The June 2023 MTFP included a £4.5m saving for PPP funding over five years. The council now states: 'It was recognised that additional budgetary provision would require to be incorporated into future MTFPs. Therefore, year three to five of this plan reflects an additional cost of £1.000 million per annum. Further additional financial consequences will be recognised in future Financial Outlooks or MTFPs.' This shows prior savings assumptions were optimistic.
findings.matters: Savings being reversed mid-plan indicates planning assumptions are unreliable. Additional costs flagged as 'will be recognised in future' suggests further increases are anticipated.
findings.figures: £4.5 million prior saving (2023), £1 million per annum additional cost (year 3–5 = £3 million additional)
findings.quote: The MTFP reported in June 2023 incorporated a saving of £4.500 million for the five years... Therefore, year three to five of this plan reflects an additional cost of £1.000 million per annum.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Council Tax increase limited to 7% in 2026/27 despite recommended 10%, constraining future increases; even 10% annual increase generates only £20.6m against £75.5m three-year gap.
findings.detail: In February 2026 the council chose to approve 7% (Band D £1,554.56) rather than recommended 10%. The document notes the council has the 4th lowest Band D charge nationally despite being 6th in deprivation, constraining political headroom for increases. Even at 10% annual increases, Council Tax would generate only £61.8m over three years—leaving £13.7m uncovered.
findings.matters: Council Tax is politically constrained and mathematically insufficient. The council cannot grow its way out of this gap; it must cut services or use reserves.
findings.figures: 7% increase approved (vs 10% recommended), Band D £1,554.56, 5–10% annual increase generates £10.3–20.6 million per year or £30.9–61.8 million over three years
findings.quote: However, at the budget setting meeting in February 2026/27 the Council took the decision to approve a 7 % increase to Council Tax, resulting in an increased Band D charge of £1,554.56.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Scottish Government may remove statutory capital accounting mitigations, creating uncertain but material additional revenue cost.
findings.detail: The council notes as a current 'notable risk': 'Scottish Government's plans to review the Capital Accounting arrangements and statutory mitigations in respect of such, to ensure they remain fit for purpose... Removing existing statutory mitigations will have material financial consequences on revenue budgets and ultimately potentially impacting on capital investment programmes.' No timetable or amount is specified, but the impact is flagged as 'material.'
findings.matters: This is an external policy change that could increase the effective budget gap by an unknown but material amount, or force capital programme cuts that damage service delivery.
findings.figures: Impact described as 'material' but unquantified
findings.quote: Removing existing statutory mitigations will have material financial consequences on revenue budgets and ultimately potentially impacting on capital investment programmes.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Council planning to hold only £25.2 million in reserves to smooth a £75.5 million three-year budget gap—reserves are finite and will be depleted.
findings.detail: The updated Reserves Policy (December 2025) recommends holding an average of the three-year budget gap (£25.181 million) to smooth delivery of savings and provide one-off investment capacity. However, this provides less than four months of the annual budget gap at the envisaged rate. Once reserves are spent, the council has no buffer for pay overruns, funding shortfalls, or savings delivery delays.
findings.matters: Reserves are temporary. If savings are not delivered, reserves will be exhausted within 2–3 years, forcing the council into a position of being unable to set a balanced budget.
findings.figures: £25.181 million targeted balance, based on average of £75.545 million three-year gap
findings.quote: Therefore, as the envisaged three year gap equates to £75.545 million, an average of £25.181 million should be targeted.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Integration Joint Board (Adult Health and Social Care) has separate budget gap of £21.7 million in 2027/28; council contribution required on top of £25 million council gap.
findings.detail: The IJB approved its own MTFP in March 2026, showing budget gaps of £21.7–22.2m per year across 2027/28–2029/30. The council must fund this from its own budget. The document explicitly reminds members: 'elected members should continue to be mindful of the Council's contribution to the IJB in support of its cost and demand pressures when settling its budget for 2027/28 and beyond.'
findings.matters: Adult care is a demand-led, unfunded service. The council cannot choose to reduce IJB funding; this is a cost it must meet, narrowing its flexibility to manage its own budget gap.
findings.figures: IJB budget gap 2027/28: £21.721 million; 2028/29: £21.820 million; 2029/30: £22.180 million
findings.quote: elected members should continue to be mindful of the Council's contribution to the IJB in support of its cost and demand pressures when settling its budget for 2027/28 and beyond

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Loan charges obligations rising by £11 million over five years; £6 million approved saving from February 2026 must now be reinstated, showing savings delivery pressure.
findings.detail: City Deal and Community Investment Programme borrowing costs are forecast at £6.39m in year 1 (£22.28m over 5 years). The council notes: 'a total increase of £11.000 million over the five years is estimated, which now also reflects the need to reinstate the loan charges funding as a result of the £6.000 million saving approved in the budget motion of February 2026.' This is a material fixed cost that cannot be avoided.
findings.matters: Reinstatement of a £6m approved saving demonstrates savings are not being achieved as planned. Fixed borrowing costs reduce flexibility to manage the budget gap elsewhere.
findings.figures: £6.390 million year 1 cost, £22.280 million over planning period, £11 million increase over 5 years, £6 million saving to be reinstated
findings.quote: There is provision for loan debt costs in relation to the Community Investment Programme, including City Deal, which equates to £6.390 million in year 1 of the plan and £22.280 million across the planning period.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Scottish Government funding assumed flat-cash, but 1% change equals £9.5 million budget impact; economic forecasters expect Local Government unlikely to be prioritised.
findings.detail: The council forecasts no real increase in core grant funding from Scottish Government, despite small cash increases announced in the Spending Review. The document notes explicitly: 'there is a risk of an actual reduction to previous cash settlements' depending on Scottish Government priorities. A 1% swing in funding creates a £9.5m budget impact, yet the forecast has no contingency for this.
findings.matters: If Scottish Government reduces funding (1% = £9.5m), the three-year budget gap widens by 12.6% or more, requiring emergency savings or accelerated reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: 1% funding change = £9.5 million impact, no assumption of additional resources above flat cash
findings.quote: Estimating future years' funding with any degree of certainty is challenging, and a slight variation on funding level can have a significant impact (1% equates to more than £9.500 million) on the Council's forecast financial position.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Pay award cost pressure of £20.6 million in 2027/28 alone, with range of £18.2 to £34.8 million depending on outcome of negotiations.
findings.detail: The council assumes 3% pay uplift for 2027/28–2028/29, reverting to 2% baseline thereafter. However, the pessimistic scenario assumes a 2.5% increase above envisaged, creating a £16.6m single-year swing. The council explicitly flags ongoing uncertainty due to economic effects of Middle East conflict. Pay is the largest single budget element; overruns cannot be absorbed elsewhere without service cuts.
findings.matters: Pay is the largest and most unpredictable cost. A pay award outcome worse than assumed would immediately worsen the budget gap by tens of millions, forcing emergency measures mid-year.
findings.figures: £20.600 million (envisaged 2027/28), £18.200 to £34.800 million (scenario range), £55.400 million (3-year envisaged)
findings.quote: a total of £20.600 million pay provision is estimated for 2027/28. Total provision over the next 3 years is anticipated to be £55.400 million.

findings.paper_title: 5 Year Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Envisaged budget gap of £114.5 million over five years, with £75.5 million in the critical three-year planning period 2027/28–2029/30.
findings.detail: This gap is before any additional Council Tax increases, approved savings, or other solutions are implemented. The council notes it is subject to ongoing review, but no specific solutions to close the gap are yet approved. Across scenario modelling, the gap ranges from £45.3m (optimistic) to £257.9m (pessimistic), demonstrating extreme sensitivity to pay and funding assumptions.
findings.matters: A gap of this magnitude cannot be closed through small efficiency savings. It requires material service reductions, significant Council Tax increases, or sustained reserve drawdown—all carrying credit and delivery risk.
findings.figures: £114.535 million (5-year), £75.545 million (3-year), range £45.336 to £257.958 million depending on scenario
findings.quote: The summary forecast envisaged position, indicates a budget gap of £114.535 million over the planning period and £75.545 million for the three-year budget period, 2027/28 to 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Housing Asset Management Plan (HAMP) 2026-2031
findings.headline: Fire safety compliance programme underway with £4.4m investment and extended sprinkler installation
findings.detail: 88 blocks identified for structural building assessment with £4.4m Scottish Government funding. 13 towers have had sprinkler systems installed; 2 more underway with completion planned January 2026. Plans call for 2 additional sprinkler systems per year across the HAMP period.
findings.matters: Ongoing fire safety regulatory compliance costs and risks across major portfolio; funding partially secured but programme extends across 5-year period
findings.figures: 88 blocks identified; £4.4m funding; 13 towers completed; 2 underway; 2/year planned
findings.quote: At present, eighty-eight blocks of properties have been identified for assessment and funding of £4.4m has been provided by the Scottish Government.

findings.paper_title: Housing Asset Management Plan (HAMP) 2026-2031
findings.headline: £807m capital and maintenance investment commitment over 5 years, funded partly through council borrowing
findings.detail: The council plans £807m investment over 2026/27-2030/31, comprising £487m capital investment and £320m repairs/maintenance. This includes £301m+ for delivery of 1,673 new homes and substantial energy efficiency retrofits. The council is using its own borrowing resources alongside grant funding (£33.655m AHSP allocation for 2025/26) to fund this multi-year programme.
findings.matters: This is a substantial multi-year financial commitment that will require sustained borrowing capacity and will impact the council's balance sheet and debt servicing obligations
findings.figures: £807m total investment; £487m capital; £320m repairs/maintenance; £301m+ for 1,673 new homes; £33.655m AHSP 2025/26
findings.quote: We plan to invest approximately £807 million in our existing housing stock over the duration of this HAMP, spanning 2026/27 to 2030/31. This includes £487 million allocated to capital investment and £320 million for repairs and maintenance.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Mears housing maintenance contractor staff changed completion dates for repair jobs; audit found scope for improved monitoring
findings.detail: A whistleblower raised concerns about the Mears Scotland LLP housing and property maintenance contract, alleging staff changed completion dates for repair jobs. Internal audit confirmed this occurred but found no direct monetary loss. However, auditors concluded there was 'significant scope for improvements' in how the service monitored and oversaw contract performance. A new Mears contract was entered for 2024/25.
findings.matters: Contractor manipulation of performance data, even without direct financial loss detected, indicates control weaknesses in a major service delivery contract; raises questions about actual service quality and whether hidden issues exist.
findings.figures: Completion date manipulation confirmed in previous Mears contract; new contract entered 2024/25
findings.quote: Internal auditors investigated and concluded that there was evidence of Mears staff changing completion dates for repair jobs. Internal auditors were satisfied that this had not resulted in any monetary loss to the council. However, internal auditors noted significant scope for improvements in how the relevant service was monitoring and overseeing performance under the contract.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Auditors found early retirement decisions for two senior officers lacked documented consideration of alternatives and value-for-money assessment
findings.detail: Two chief officers were granted early retirement in 2024/25 as part of restructuring that reduced chief officers from six to five. Auditors found that while alternatives were reportedly considered, this was documented as 'not applicable' with insufficient clarity on why alternatives were rejected or how value-for-money was assessed. Auditors recommended enhanced scrutiny and transparency, and the council plans a governance review by December 2026.
findings.matters: Lack of transparent decision documentation on senior exit costs raises questions about financial controls, governance rigour, and whether the council is achieving value-for-money in employment decisions.
findings.figures: Two chief officers early retirement; chief officer headcount reduced by one
findings.quote: auditors found that it was not always clear how the council had considered whether alternative options to early retirement would have: been feasible; and/or represented better value for money.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Council increased council tax by 10% in 2025/26, highest in recent years, to bridge modest budget gap
findings.detail: To address a 2025/26 General Fund budget gap of £13.6 million (1.2% of budget), the council raised council tax by 10%, significantly higher than the 5% increase in 2023/24 or 3% in 2022/23. This steep rise to solve a relatively small gap suggests limited headroom for future tax increases to close the larger gaps projected ahead.
findings.matters: Double-digit council tax increases signal taxpayer tolerance limits and constrain a council's primary revenue-raising tool; if 10% was necessary for a 1.2% gap, future larger gaps cannot be solved by tax alone.
findings.figures: 10% council tax increase for 2025/26 (£15.3m revenue); compares to 5% in 2023/24, 3% in 2022/23
findings.quote: The council increased council tax by ten per cent to bridge the budget gap for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Capital spend falling short of plans; council increases borrowing by £99 million while reprofiling delivery
findings.detail: Capital spending has been consistently lower than planned, driven by inflation and construction sector constraints. The council reprofiled £15.7 million from 2024/25 to later years of its five-year programme while increasing long-term borrowing from £590.6 million (March 2024) to £689.6 million (March 2025). The £856 million five-year capital investment programme is planned but delivery risk is evident.
findings.matters: Persistent capital underperformance combined with increased borrowing signals both project delivery challenges and rising debt service costs; escalating borrowing to fund delayed programmes increases refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Long-term borrowing increased £99m (£590.6m to £689.6m); £856m capital planned 2024/25–2028/29; £15.7m reprofiled from 2024/25
findings.quote: Capital spend has been lower than planned in recent years. A number of external factors have contributed to this, including inflationary pressures and availability of materials and labour in the construction industry.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Adult social care performance significantly weaker than other services; only 18% of indicators in top two quartiles
findings.detail: Performance across Local Government Benchmarking Framework indicators is mixed. Adult social work services performance is particularly weak, with only 18% of indicators in the top two quartiles versus 100% for housing and 50% for the council overall. The council has also seen sustained deterioration in satisfaction indicators since 2010/11, a 15-year downward trend that should concern any service user base assessment.
findings.matters: Weakening performance in demand-led services like adult social care often signals growing unmet need or service quality issues, both of which have budget implications and reputational risk; deteriorating satisfaction trends suggest eroding public confidence.
findings.figures: Adult social work: 18% of indicators in top two quartiles; satisfaction indicators declined since 2010/11 baseline
findings.quote: only 18 per cent of indicators for Adult social work services remain in the top two quartiles.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Reserves policy requires strategic review; council holds £282 million earmarked but strategy for use unclear
findings.detail: The council holds £346.3 million in total usable reserves, with £282.0 million earmarked for future budget pressures. The Accounts Commission specifically required the council to address auditor recommendations 'around reviewing its approach to the use of reserves' and 'to now set out clearly how it intends to close the budget gap'. The council has committed to a reserves review by June 2026. This signals auditor concern that reserves are being managed tactically rather than strategically.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on reserves to manage recurring budget gaps indicates the council is not living within sustainable revenue income; unclear strategy for reserve drawdown creates uncertainty about medium-term solvency.
findings.figures: £346.3m total usable reserves (2024/25); £282.0m earmarked General Fund balance
findings.quote: The council will need to ensure that it applies its reserves strategically. This will include reviewing how its reserves earmarked for future budget pressures can be used to support investment in long-term sustainability or improved outcomes.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Council's primary mitigation strategy—transformation—acknowledged to be insufficient to close budget gap alone
findings.detail: The council is investing £793.1 million through its Community Investment Fund (through 2033/34) and embedding transformation across all services. However, officers have explicitly stated transformation will not close the budget gap. The Accounts Commission emphasises that benefits realisation is 'essential' given the 'increasing role that transformation needs to play in closing the budget gap'—signalling the Commission's concern that the council is relying on a strategy it knows is inadequate.
findings.matters: If the council cannot articulate how it will deliver the necessary savings beyond transformation, there is material execution risk to achieving financial sustainability and meeting loan covenants.
findings.figures: £793.1 million Community Investment Fund value through 2033/34
findings.quote: officers are clear that transformation will not close the budget gap alone.

findings.paper_title: North Lanarkshire Council Best Value Controller of Audit Report
findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £136.9 million over five years with no clear strategy articulated to close it
findings.detail: The council faces a General Fund cumulative budget gap of £136.9 million from 2026/27 to 2030/31 based on flat cash settlement, on top of the £20.6 million gap for 2025/26. The Controller of Audit explicitly states it is not yet clear how the council will address the widening gap. This becomes critical given the scale of the challenge and the inadequacy of current mitigation plans.
findings.matters: Lenders need confidence that a council can achieve financial sustainability; a widening gap with no articulated solution is a red flag for service continuity and debt service risk.
findings.figures: £136.9m cumulative 2026/27–2030/31; £20.6m for 2025/26 (General Fund £13.6m + HRA £7.0m)
findings.quote: it is not yet clear how the council will fully address it. Given the scale of emerging challenges and the widening budget gap, a strategic shift is now essential to ensure continued financial sustainability and service delivery.

findings.paper_title: Review of 2025/26 to 2027/28 Budget Savings
findings.headline: 2026/27 shows 23% of approved savings unachieved (£0.323m gap), repeating the pattern from 2025/26
findings.detail: Council approved £1.393m in 2026/27 savings but projects only £1.070m (77%) delivery, leaving a £0.323m gap. While council states these will be achieved in later years, the pattern of failing to deliver savings on the scheduled timeline persists into the second year of the three-year plan.
findings.matters: Consecutive years of savings shortfalls suggest structural issues with savings delivery capability or forecasting realism, affecting confidence in multi-year budget stability and financial recovery plans
findings.figures: £1.393m approved, £1.070m projected (77%), £0.323m gap
findings.quote: It is currently anticipated that £1.070m (77%) of approved 2026/27 savings of £1.393m will be achieved in the 2026/27 financial year, leaving an in-year savings gap of £0.323m.

findings.paper_title: Review of 2025/26 to 2027/28 Budget Savings
findings.headline: Two major operational savings totalling £0.373m are projected to deliver zero benefit in 2025/26
findings.detail: Fleet MOT rationalisation (£0.200m approved) and Asset Management/Office Disinvestment (£0.173m approved) within Enterprise & Communities are both showing £0.000m projected delivery. These were expected to yield material operational savings but have completely failed to materialize on the planned schedule.
findings.matters: Large scheduled savings that yield no benefit indicate delivery challenges or unrealistic budgeting, undermining the credibility of future savings forecasts and multi-year budget plans
findings.figures: £0.200m (Fleet MOTs), £0.173m (Asset Management rationalisation)
findings.quote: E&C Community Operations Fleet MOT's 0.200 0.000 0.200 0.000; E&C Assets & Procurement Asset Management Rationalisation/Office Dis-investment. 0.173 0.000 0.173 0.000

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Activity Report 2025/26
findings.headline: The council has provided a financial guarantee covering up to 80% of debt service costs (£30m facility) to North Lanarkshire Properties LLP
findings.detail: In 2023/24, the council agreed to guarantee up to 80% of debt service costs on a £30m refinancing facility for North Lanarkshire Properties LLP. While the council considers the likelihood of the guarantee being called 'minimal', a financial guarantee is a contingent liability. The council made a provision of £0.825m and is receiving annual premiums (£0.167m in 2025/26) to offset the risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand contingent liabilities. If NLP LLP's finances deteriorate, the council could be called to cover up to £24m in debt service costs (80% of £30m).
findings.figures: Guarantee limit: 80% of £30m facility = up to £24m exposure. Initial provision: £0.825m. Premium received 2025/26: £0.167m. Long-term debtor: £0.255m; short-term debtor: £0.164m.
findings.quote: In 2023/24, the Council agreed to provide a new financial guarantee to North Lanarkshire Properties LLP (NLP LLP) as part of re-financing arrangements undertaken by NLP LLP, with the Council providing underwriting of debt service costs, up to a limit of 80% of the total debt service costs of the new long-term facility of £30.0m.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Activity Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Economic volatility and potential interest rate hikes pose risks to future borrowing costs
findings.detail: The report documents significant economic uncertainty, including the US/Israel-Iran war's impact on commodity and oil prices, persistent inflation concerns (3% CPI in February 2026), and a weak labour market. While the Bank of England cut rates to 3.75% by December 2025, March 2026 saw rates held and potential upside risks to inflation. Treasury advisors predict Base Rate will remain at 3.75%, but note 'highly uncertain' outlooks with potential for rate hikes.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether borrowing costs have bottomed or whether the council faces higher refinancing costs. Inflation and potential rate hikes directly increase the cost of new borrowing needed for the capital programme.
findings.figures: Base Rate: held at 3.75% from December 2025. 10-year gilt yield: started at 4.65%, ended at 4.86%. PWLB 10-year rate: 5.38% at start, 5.72% at end of year.
findings.quote: The MPC noted the risks to both inflation and growth and indicated they could move rates either up or down depending on the conditions. Financial markets quickly responded to this by pricing in rate hikes. Following the March MPC meeting, our treasury management advisors revised its central interest rate view and now predicts Base Rate will be held at 3.75%. However, the conflict makes the outlook for rates highly uncertain.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Activity Report 2025/26
findings.headline: The council forecasts substantial new borrowing requirements over the next five years—£433m to £1.56bn cumulatively
findings.detail: The Liability Benchmark analysis (section 9.11-9.13) projects that the council will require significant new borrowing to fund its approved capital programme. New borrowing needed rises from zero in 2026/27 to £433m in 2027, £805m in 2028, and £1.56bn by 2030/31. This reflects the scale of the capital investment programme and declining available reserves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's medium-term borrowing trajectory. This forecast indicates sustained heavy borrowing to fund capital, raising questions about long-term sustainability and debt capacity.
findings.quote: The Loans CFR (solid light blue) represents the total cost of the capital expenditure plans based on the estimated current profile of the 5-year Capital Programme 2024/2025 to 2028/2029 as approved by Policy & Strategy Committee on 6th March 2026. The gap between the grey section and the liability benchmark line represents the estimated additional borrowing that is forecast will be required to fund the current capital expenditure plans, via long-term and short-term borrowing options.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Activity Report 2025/26
findings.headline: A LOBO loan carrying 10.937% interest is callable within the next 12 months
findings.detail: The council holds a £1.0m LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loan originated in the mid-1980s to early 1990s with a call date falling within one year. The interest rate on this loan is 10.937%—substantially above current market rates. While the council assesses the risk of the lender exercising the call option as 'minimal', if called, the council would either have to accept refinancing at current rates or repay the loan, creating a refinancing risk.
findings.matters: A LOBO call can force refinancing at unfavourable rates and create unexpected cash demands. The 10.937% rate shows historical expensive debt that may be called; this is a contingent liability.
findings.figures: LOBO exposure: £1.0m at 10.937% interest. Call date: within 12 months of 31 March 2026 (i.e., by 31 March 2027). Loan origination: mid-1980s to early 1990s.
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026 the Council had an exposure of £1.0m to LOBO loans, which has a call date falling within less than one year, with interest rates payable of 10.937%. This balance of £1.0m was taken out in the mid 1980's to early 1990's. Based on the current and the forecast interest rates the likelihood of these loans being called has been assessed as minimal.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Activity Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Interest payments are rising despite lower interest rates, increasing the cost of debt service
findings.detail: Interest payments rose from £57.2m in 2024/25 to £60.4m in 2025/26—an increase of £3.2m. While the council achieved savings on new borrowing due to lower rates (4.50% vs estimated 5.85%), the overall portfolio cost continues to increase. The weighted average loans fund pool rate decreased only marginally from 4.87% to 4.78%.
findings.matters: Rising interest costs reduce resources available for services. A lender examining repayment capacity needs to know whether interest costs are stabilising or accelerating.
findings.figures: Interest payments 2025/26: £60.4m (up from £57.2m in 2024/25). Weighted average loans pool rate: 4.78% vs 4.87% prior year. External interest payable: £64.0m (actual vs £65.0m estimate).
findings.quote: The Council made interest payments in 2025/2026 of £60.4m (£57.2m in 2024/2025). This includes both the external and internal elements of interest payable, and the annual write-off associated with premiums and discounts. This increase of £10.4m from 2024/2025 levels represents additional net interest costs of £3.2m

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Activity Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Debt has risen by £115.7m in one year, driven by PWLB borrowing to fund capital investment
findings.detail: Total external debt increased from £1,284.5m to £1,400.2m during 2025/26. The increase was primarily driven by new PWLB borrowing of £185.0m offset by £77.0m in PWLB repayments, plus an £8.0m increase in temporary borrowing. The council is relying heavily on PWLB as its primary borrowing source (58.4% of total debt).
findings.matters: A lender needs to track debt trajectory and borrowing concentration. PWLB dependency matters if government policy changes; the sharp increase signals growing reliance on external finance.
findings.figures: Total external debt £1,400.2m at 31 March 2026 vs £1,284.5m at 31 March 2025. PWLB borrowing: £818.1m (58.4% of total debt). New PWLB borrowing £185.0m in 2025/26.
findings.quote: At the 31 March 2026 the Council's total external debt, defined as actual gross borrowing (excluding interest accrued) plus obligations outstanding in respect of finance leases including IFRS16 and Service Concessions liabilities had risen from £1,284.5m to £1,400.2m, an increase of £115.7m

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Activity Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital programme delivery is under sustained pressure from material costs and contractor capacity
findings.detail: The council experienced ongoing challenges delivering its strategic capital investment and HRA programmes throughout 2025/26. External economic factors—particularly material availability, contractor capacity, and inflationary pressures—are reducing delivery timelines. The council has had to reprofile the capital programme multiple times during the year (March, August, October 2025 and January 2026) to reflect revised delivery expectations.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's capital programme is genuinely deliverable or if slippage is structural; delayed capital schemes can affect service provision and council revenue.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure of £322.8m in 2025/26, compared to initial estimate of £293.6m and revised estimate of £323.6m
findings.quote: The Council continued to experience challenges in delivering the Strategic Capital Investment Programme and HRA Investment Programme in light of a number of external factors affecting the wider economy including availability of materials, contractors and inflationary pressures. This resulted in reduced capacity for external contractors to deliver projects within previously assumed timelines, and increased material costs.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring Report for Quarter ended 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Operational boundary for long-term liabilities breached, though noted as immaterial
findings.detail: The operational boundary limit for long-term liabilities was exceeded by £0.6m at quarter-end due to IFRS16 remeasurement of PPP liabilities. The report notes this is not significant as the operational boundary is a management tool, but it shows the council operating closer to its prudential limits.
findings.matters: Even minor boundary breaches signal the council is operating with tighter prudential headroom. Lenders track whether councils are staying comfortably within their own limits as a management quality indicator.
findings.figures: Breach: £0.6m over operational boundary
findings.quote: Whilst the Operational Boundary limit for Long-term liabilities was exceeded by £0.6m, this was due to IFRS16 remeasurement of PPP liabilities at 25/26 year-end, slightly higher than envisaged at TMS when the limits were set.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring Report for Quarter ended 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing costs rising: average rate increased from 4.31% to 4.41%
findings.detail: The cost of temporary borrowing to cover cash flow has increased by 10 basis points in the quarter, with short-term loans now at 4.41% average rate on a £236m portfolio. This reflects the council's reliance on rolling short-term borrowing in a rising rate environment.
findings.matters: Reliance on short-term borrowing exposes the council to refinancing risk if rates remain elevated or spike further. A lender will want to track whether the council is moving to longer-term fixed borrowing to reduce this exposure.
findings.quote: The average rate on the Council's current short-term loans portfolio of £236.0m at 30th June 2026 was 4.41%, this compares with 4.31% on £228.0m loans in the previous quarter.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring Report for Quarter ended 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Council is actively assessing whether capital programme remains sustainably affordable
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it has undertaken an assessment due to 'current financial volatility and increased borrowing costs' to determine if the five-year capital programme needs further review to remain sustainably affordable. This assessment is ongoing.
findings.matters: This signals the council recognises fiscal pressure and may cut or defer capital projects. A lender funding existing borrowing needs to know if future capital projects could be scaled back, affecting the council's infrastructure and service capacity.
findings.figures: None given for possible reductions
findings.quote: However, the current financial volatility and increased borrowing costs has resulted in an assessment being undertaken of the potential impact on future years of the current capital programme. This will continue to be monitored to determine if any further review of the programme is required to ensure that it remains sustainably affordable.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring Report for Quarter ended 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Financing costs rising steeply as proportion of revenue: HRA to reach 35% by 2031
findings.detail: For the Housing Revenue Account, financing costs are projected to rise from 24.9% of net revenue stream in 2026/27 to 35.1% by 2030/31. General Fund financing costs also rising from 5.4% to 8.3% over the same period. This leaves limited flexibility for service delivery or responding to shocks.
findings.matters: A lender assesses debt serviceability by looking at what proportion of revenue is consumed by debt costs. At 35% for HRA, the council is approaching levels where debt repayment becomes the dominant budget item.
findings.quote: Proportion of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream - HRA 24.9% 25.0% 0.1% 26.7% 29.9% 33.0% 35.1%

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring Report for Quarter ended 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Loan charges increased £4.7m against budget due to higher interest rates and internal charges
findings.detail: The council's projected treasury costs are now £4.7m higher than initially estimated, primarily from rising market interest rates and higher internal Interest on Revenue Balances (IORB) charges. This remains within budget but represents material pressure.
findings.matters: Rising financing costs reduce headroom for other council services and indicate interest rate sensitivity; a lender will want to track whether this trend continues.
findings.figures: Loan charge variance: £4.7m increase; General Fund increased spend £4.5m, HRA £0.3m
findings.quote: Indicator 2(b) highlights a projected increase in loan charges of £4.7m compared to the initial Treasury Management Strategy estimates for 2026/27. This projection takes account of treasury management activity, internal Interest on Revenue Balances (IORB) recharges due to increased market interest rates

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring Report for Quarter ended 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Projected new borrowing requirement of £397.1m–£1.5bn over next five years
findings.detail: The liability benchmark shows the council will need to borrow significantly beyond existing debt to fund approved capital and revenue plans. New borrowing required is £397.1m in 2027/28, rising to £1,547.2m by 2030/31. This assumes all cash reserves are used to offset requirements.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the magnitude of future funding need and whether the council can sustainably service this debt trajectory.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme 2026/27 Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Capital programme delivery faces material headwinds from economic climate affecting material and contractor availability
findings.detail: The council's risk assessment identifies wider economic climate factors—material scarcity, contractor availability, and inflationary pressure—as active threats to capital programme delivery. These are being tracked by Project Boards.
findings.matters: External supply-side constraints on a council's capital programme are largely outside management control and can cause project delays or cost overruns.
findings.figures: Risk management through SCDG Terms of Reference; no financial quantification provided
findings.quote: the capital programme continues to face challenges in relation to the wider economic climate, linked to availability of materials, contractors and inflationary pressures

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme 2026/27 Monitoring Report
findings.headline: A systematic 10% downward adjustment to the capital programme reflects historic profiling failures in project delivery
findings.detail: The council applies a 10% trend-based adjustment (£15.183m on General Services) to account for consistent under-delivery caused by procurement delays, contractor issues, and site conditions. This adjustment informs Treasury borrowing forecasts.
findings.matters: Systematic project slippage indicates capital delivery is slower than planned, creating cash flow volatility and potential for higher peak borrowing than originally forecast.
findings.figures: Trend adjustment of £15.183m applied to working programme of £185.183m (8.2%)
findings.quote: A 10% Trend-Based Adjustment has been applied to the General Services Capital Programme to reflect historic profiling challenges in delivering major capital projects, often caused by procurement challenges, contractor issues, and site conditions

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme 2026/27 Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Capital cost inflation creating ongoing challenges for all service areas to deliver programmes within available resources
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that continuing increases in capital delivery costs are causing significant challenges across all services in managing capital programmes within available budgets. Services are required to manage this within existing resources.
findings.matters: Persistent cost pressures may force scope reductions or delays; councils unable to absorb cost inflation risk programme underspend or deferred investment.
findings.figures: General Services programme £170.000m; HRA programme £169.007m; combined requiring £214.623m borrowing
findings.quote: with continuing increases in the cost of delivering capital programmes all service areas continue to face significant challenges managing the delivery of capital programmes within the available envelope of resources

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026/27 to 2028/29 and Council Tax 2026/27
findings.headline: Significant additional Adult Health and Social Care spending (£25.050 million) is entirely directed/ring-fenced funding, creating dependency on continued government allocation
findings.detail: The budget includes £25.050 million additional spending for Adult Health and Social Care: £11.283 million for free personal care uprating and social care living wage support, and £13.767 million from changes to funding distribution methodology. This entire sum is directed or ring-fenced from Scottish Government, meaning the council cannot redeploy it and is vulnerable to future allocation changes.
findings.matters: While currently funded, this large directed commitment constrains budgetary flexibility and exposes the council to risk if funding distributions change, funding is clawed back, or if social care cost pressures exceed the allocated amount.
findings.figures: £25.050 million total Adult Health & Social Care funding: £11.283 million directed (free personal care and living wage); £13.767 million from methodology change
findings.quote: Additional directed funding of £11.283 million associated with the uprating of free personal care and to support the continuation of the living wage for social care provision. Secondly, additional funding of circa £13.767 million following changes to the funding distribution methodology incorporated into the local government settlement for older adult services.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026/27 to 2028/29 and Council Tax 2026/27
findings.headline: Contingency reserve policy change increases minimum holding by £3.800 million, reducing flexibility for one-off investment
findings.detail: The revised Reserves Policy requires the contingency reserve to be held at 1% of net revenue budget rather than a static £8 million, increasing it to c. £11.800 million. Combined with a target of £23.500 million for Future Budget Challenges, this leaves only c. £10.413 million available for other one-off investment from a total Future Budget Pressures balance of £37.713 million.
findings.matters: The increase in minimum reserves constrains the council's ability to respond to emerging pressures or fund one-off transformation costs, reducing financial flexibility precisely when the multi-year budget gap is widest.
findings.figures: Contingency reserve increases from £8 million to c. £11.800 million (increase of £3.800 million). Future Budget Challenges target £23.500 million. Available for one-off investment only c. £10.413 million.
findings.quote: the revised contingency will require to be c. £11.800 million, based on the budgeted expenditure within this report, which is an increase of £3.800 million.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026/27 to 2028/29 and Council Tax 2026/27
findings.headline: Pay cost risk: 2025/26 settlements already exceed the annual average assumed in planning, putting 3% assumption at risk for years 2 and 3
findings.detail: The council's Medium-Term Financial Plan assumes 3% annual pay awards, aligned with the Public Sector Pay Policy maximum of 9% over three years. However, pay settlements agreed in 2025/26 have already exceeded this annual average. The council assumes Scottish Government will fund any award greater than 3%, but this is not guaranteed and could materialize as an unplanned cost pressure.
findings.matters: Pay is the largest expenditure category; unfunded pay awards would immediately trigger new deficits requiring emergency savings or reserve drawdown, both of which are already constrained.
findings.figures: 2025/26 and 2026/27 pay awards total £9.465 million. Planning assumption 3% annually; Public Sector Pay Policy 9% over 3 years (3% average). 2025/26 settlements already above this.
findings.quote: However, pay settlements agreed during 2025/26 are already above the annual average as set out in the policy. Therefore, there is a risk that could be repeated in years two and three of the policy, thus putting this financial planning assumption at risk.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026/27 to 2028/29 and Council Tax 2026/27
findings.headline: Change Management Fund forecast to turn negative by 2028/29, indicating unsustainable trajectory for one-off savings costs
findings.detail: The fund supporting one-off costs of approved and future savings is projected to close 2027/28 at £7.553 million but then deteriorate to negative £2.447 million in 2028/29, falling to negative £14.847 million by 2030/31. The council is releasing £10 million from the Future Budget Pressures reserve during 2026/27 to fund one-off investment.
findings.matters: Negative reserves force the council to either accelerate recurring savings, draw on general contingency, or leave savings unimplemented. This materially increases delivery risk in years 3–5.
findings.quote: Forecast Closing Balance 7.553 3.953 (2.447) (8.947) (14.847)

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026/27 to 2028/29 and Council Tax 2026/27
findings.headline: Three-year budget gap of £70.584 million dependent on Council Tax increases of 10% for 2026/27–2027/28 and 5% in 2028/29
findings.detail: The council faces a revised budget shortfall of £19.273 million for 2026/27, rising to £25.956 million and £25.355 million in subsequent years. The Section 95 Officer recommends Council Tax increases to protect services, with each 1% increase generating c. £1.872 million. The budget strategy explicitly assumes these increases are necessary to close the gap.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's fiscal plan relies on tax increases that may face political resistance, caps, or community opposition, and whether savings delivery is otherwise credible.
findings.figures: £19.273 million gap 2026/27, £25.956 million 2027/28, £25.355 million 2028/29 (total £70.584 million). Planned Council Tax increases 10%, 10%, 5%. 1% increase = c. £1.872 million
findings.quote: Subsequently, the Section 95 Officer presented an update on the Council Tax Strategy to Policy and Strategy Committee in December 2025, with a similar approach recommended for the 2026/27 to 2028/29 three-year budget, in order to protect vital public services valued by local communities i.e.10% Council Tax increase for the next two years, and 5% in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: HRA Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: High-speed internet rollout to all 36,000 social housing properties is forecasted to cost £4.183m cumulatively with loan charges plus operational costs, but full programme scope and payback from smart technology fault detection remain unconfirmed.
findings.detail: An initial pilot covering 1,932 properties is underway. The plan assumes phased rollout to remaining stock with estimated costs of £0.581m to £1.018m annually (combining loan charges and operations). A separate test-of-change programme for smart detection technology is being funded from earmarked reserves, with full rollout costs and benefits to be determined in future plan iterations.
findings.matters: Significant ongoing operational and financing costs for infrastructure with unproven financial benefits. Expected savings from fault detection are not yet quantified, creating risk of sunk costs with limited offsetting revenue benefit.
findings.quote: The 2026/27 plan included provision for the installation of high-speed internet to all social housing stock. An initial pilot, covering 1,932 properties, is currently underway with a number of homes already connected and operational. This plan assumes a phased rollout to the remaining housing stock. It is anticipated this would allow early detection of faults preventing more costly repairs being required over time.

findings.paper_title: HRA Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: The plan does not assume any rent level for future years, leaving the critical tool for closing the £53m budget gap completely unresolved and subject to future political and tenant affordability decisions.
findings.detail: The financial forecast models cost pressures without specifying what rent increases will be set to fund them. The plan notes that rent-setting decisions in 2027/28 will have cascading impacts on future year cost pressures, but provides no guidance on the rent trajectory required to balance the budget. This creates a significant gap between the modelled costs and the assumed revenue.
findings.matters: The plan's internal logic is incomplete: cost pressures are quantified but revenue assumptions are deferred. Lenders cannot assess financial resilience without knowing assumed rent levels. Political pressure may prevent rent increases sufficient to match cost growth.
findings.figures: £53.155m budget gap; rent level assumptions: unspecified
findings.quote: The plan does not make an assumption on the level of rents that will be set when presenting the financial cost pressures. As Committee will be aware, decisions taken in setting the 2027/28 revenue estimates will have an impact on future year cost pressures and rent charges.

findings.paper_title: HRA Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Unallocated reserves of only £9.178m remain after contingency and earmarked allocations, providing limited buffer against cost volatility or unexpected pressures over a £53m five-year budget gap.
findings.detail: Total HRA reserves are £25.098m, but £2.007m is ring-fenced as 1% contingency and £13.913m is earmarked for specific purposes, leaving only £9.178m available. The plan states that using reserves for recurring expenditure is unsustainable and requires evidence of permanent solutions. No reserve drawdown is assumed to balance the budget.
findings.matters: Limited financial flexibility to absorb unexpected cost overruns or interest rate shocks. The gap between unallocated reserves (£9.178m) and annual budget pressures (£7–13m per year) means any extended period of adverse variance would rapidly deplete contingency.
findings.figures: Total reserves £25.098m; contingency £2.007m; earmarked £13.913m; unallocated £9.178m
findings.quote: The HRA currently hold reserves totalling of £25.098m brought forward from 2025/26. After accounting for the contingency fund representing 1% of the HRA budget and for funds held for specific purposes, a total of £9.178m remains unallocated. Reserve balances represent one-off funding and using reserves for recurring expenditure or to balance the budget is not sustainable.

findings.paper_title: HRA Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Grounds maintenance costs are escalating £0.453m annually due to exit of larger contractors from the market, forcing procurement from multiple smaller suppliers at higher unit cost, with further pressures anticipated from tower reprovisioning.
findings.detail: The council previously contracted with larger grounds maintenance providers who have now exited the market. The council must now procure services from multiple smaller suppliers to meet demand, eliminating economies of scale and raising unit costs. The plan notes that housing stock composition changes—particularly the tower reprovisioning programme—may generate additional undefined cost pressures.
findings.matters: Market structure changes creating cost inflation outside the council's direct control. Undefined future pressures from tower reprovisioning strategy introduce unquantified risk to the plan.
findings.figures: £0.453m additional cost pressure identified; further costs from tower reprovisioning not yet quantified
findings.quote: An additional cost pressure of £0.453m has been identified in relation to grounds maintenance and care of gardens. This increase is primarily attributable to the exit of larger providers from the market. As a result, contracts are now being procured on a smaller scale across multiple suppliers to meet service demand, leading to higher unit costs due to the loss of economies of scale.

findings.paper_title: HRA Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Housing repairs contract costs are forecast at £9.572m cumulatively over the plan period, accounting for 38% of HRA expenditure and subject to external indexation (BCIS then CPI+1%) largely outside council control.
findings.detail: Repairs account for more than one-third of HRA spending. An 8-year contract commenced July 2024 uses BCIS indexing (4% assumed for 2027/28) then CPI+1% for remaining years. Annual costs range £1.288m to £2.323m. The plan notes the market for repairs has changed, with larger providers exiting, increasing procurement complexity and cost volatility.
findings.matters: Repairs represent the single largest controllable cost after borrowing. Indexation formulas limit flexibility; if actual inflation exceeds CPI+1%, budget shortfalls cascade.
findings.quote: The largest area of spend for the HRA is for repairs and maintenance of the Council's housing stock... A combined contract for Housing Repairs with a minimum term of 8 years commenced from 1 July 2024. The contract is subject to annual inflation applied to the schedule of rates based on the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors' Building Cost Information Services' General Building Cost Index (BCIS).

findings.paper_title: HRA Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Borrowing costs will increase by £44.15m cumulatively over the plan period (from £3.441m to £12.061m annually) due to ambitious capital investment, with extreme sensitivity to interest rates: a 1% rate change swings costs by £7–8m annually.
findings.detail: The HRA is pursuing a £168m capital programme for 2026/27 alone, covering housing stock improvements and new supply. This drives escalating borrowing costs: £3.441m in 2027/28, peaking at £12.061m in 2028/29. Sensitivity analysis shows a 1% increase in interest rates would add £7.791m in 2027/28, while a 1% decrease would save £7.721m. The plan relies on earmarked reserves to smooth rate volatility, but acknowledges high uncertainty from external economic factors.
findings.matters: Borrowing costs are the largest single driver of the budget gap (41% of total pressures over 5 years). The council's financial plan is hostage to interest rates it cannot control; rate movements dwarf annual cost savings initiatives.
findings.quote: Based on the current investment targets for the next 5 years, it is anticipated that the HRA will incur additional borrowing costs of £3.441m in 2027/28 with a further £12.061m in 2028/29, £10.005m in 2029/30, £9.649m in 2030/31 and £8.998m in 2031/32. A 1% increase in the interest rate for 2027/28 would result in an additional £7.791m cost pressure.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Report Council Summary - 1 April 2026 to 19 June 2026
findings.headline: Property costs in Enterprise and Communities overspend by £0.239m, with electricity costs at the new Bellshill Hub under investigation
findings.detail: Property costs are forecasted to overspend by £0.239m, primarily reflecting forecast increased electricity costs at the new Bellshill Hub which are being investigated. An additional £0.159m overspend on external vehicle hire is based on anticipated demand. The council is still at an early stage of understanding these cost drivers.
findings.matters: Unexplained cost pressures on new facilities, especially utilities, can indicate operational, design, or occupancy issues; ongoing investigation suggests costs may move further if root causes are not understood
findings.figures: £0.239m property cost overspend (Bellshill Hub electricity); £0.159m external vehicle hire overspend
findings.quote: overspends in Property costs of £0.23 9m primarily reflecting forecast increased electricity costs associated with the new Bellshill Hub which are being investigated and external vehicle hire costs based on anticipated demand (£0.159m)

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Report Council Summary - 1 April 2026 to 19 June 2026
findings.headline: Enterprise and Communities shows an income under-recovery of £0.315m linked to capital recharge and parking charge shortfalls
findings.detail: Enterprise and Communities is reporting breakeven overall, but masks an under-recovery in income of £0.315m resulting from capital recharge under-recovery linked to vacancy savings and an under-recovery of parking charge income. This suggests both internal pricing issues and potential demand weakness in parking.
findings.matters: Parking income shortfalls and capital recharge under-recovery can signal economic headwinds affecting foot traffic and activity, or pricing/cost allocation problems; both warrant close monitoring
findings.figures: £0.315m under-recovery in income; comprises capital recharge under-recovery and parking charge income shortfall
findings.quote: In addition, an under-recovery in income of £0.315m is projected as a result of capital recharge under -recovery linked to vacancy savings together with an under-recovery of parking charge income.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Report Council Summary - 1 April 2026 to 19 June 2026
findings.headline: Approved savings of £2.915m will only be 88% delivered in-year, with replacement savings identified for the £0.350m gap
findings.detail: The council approved savings of £2.915m for 2026/27. At Q1, only £2.565m (88%) is projected to be achieved in the current year, with replacement savings of £0.350m identified in-year to cover the shortfall. This indicates that not all planned savings are materialising from their original sources.
findings.matters: Incomplete delivery of planned savings suggests either optimistic initial budgeting or service pressures preventing expected reductions; reliance on replacement savings instead of original targets raises questions about long-term budget sustainability
findings.figures: £2.915m savings target; £2.565m projected delivery (88%); £0.350m replacement savings identified
findings.quote: It is projected that £ 2.565m of savings (88%) will be achieved in the current year, with replacement savings of £0.350m identified in year to fully address the shortfall.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Report Council Summary - 1 April 2026 to 19 June 2026
findings.headline: Adult Health and Social Care is overspending by £2.627m, driven by increased demand in care homes and at-home provision
findings.detail: The council's contribution to the Integration Joint Board is projecting an overspend of £2.627m at Q1. This is primarily driven by £4.436m of overspends in payments to other bodies and transfer payments, linked to increased demand in Care at Home and Independent Care homes, plus expenditure on winter planning initiatives. This is partially offset by underspends in employee costs (£0.996m) and over-recovery of income (£0.893m).
findings.matters: Demand-driven pressures in adult social care are structural and difficult to control; a growing shortfall here signals rising community need and a potential funding squeeze if the trend continues through the year
findings.figures: £2.627m overspend; £4.436m in payments to other bodies and transfer payments; £0.996m employee cost underspend; £0.893m income over-recovery
findings.quote: Council Adult Health and Social Care provision to the Integration Joint Board (IJB) is projecting an overall overspend of £ 2.627m primarily as a result of overspends in payments to other bodies and transfer payments of £4.436m linked to increased demand in Care at Home and Independent Care homes along with expenditure linked to winter planning initiatives

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/2027 Treasury Management and Prudential Indicators 2026/2027 to 2030/2031
findings.headline: IFRS16 lease accounting added £93.6m to debt in 2024/25 with ongoing impacts
findings.detail: The implementation of IFRS16 Leases accounting in 2024/25 increased the council's Capital Financing Requirement by £93.6m in that year (PPP £88.2m, property £2.9m, vehicles £2.5m). Going forward, annual lease liability recalculations of £19.9m are built into the capital plans, but this is an accounting, not cash, impact.
findings.matters: While lease accounting is non-cash, it materially increases measured debt levels, which affects prudential indicators and debt ratios used by lenders. The £88.2m PPP element represents long-term service concession liabilities that must be serviced from revenue.
findings.figures: IFRS16 impact in 2024/25: £93.6m total (PPP £88.2m, property £2.9m, VPE £2.5m); ongoing annual lease recalculations £19.9m
findings.quote: Following implementation of IFRS16 Leases in 2024/2025 financial year, primarily impacting upon the accounting treatment for operational property and vehicles, plant and equipment (VPE), acquired under operating lease arrangements , as well as impacting on PPP contract liabilities , with an increase in the Council's 2024/2025 Capital Financing Requirement of £93.6m (PPP £88.2m, Property £2.9m & VPE £2.5m).

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/2027 Treasury Management and Prudential Indicators 2026/2027 to 2030/2031
findings.headline: All new borrowing will be at fixed rates averaging 4.55-5.45% over the forecast period
findings.detail: The council intends to finance its capital programme entirely with fixed-rate debt. PWLB rates are forecast to average 4.59%-5.74% depending on maturity, with the 5-year rate averaging 4.55%-4.60% and the 50-year rate 5.38%-5.45% after applying the certainty rate discount. This provides certainty but locks in rising rates.
findings.matters: Locking in rates at 4.6%-5.7% eliminates interest rate risk but commits the council to paying these rates even if Bank Rate falls further. Given the council's rising debt levels, small interest rate changes have material cash impacts (£2m per 1% movement in 2026/27).
findings.figures: 5-year PWLB rate 4.55%-4.60%; 50-year rate 5.38%-5.45%; interest sensitivity ±1% = £2.0m impact on 2026/27 net loan interest

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/2027 Treasury Management and Prudential Indicators 2026/2027 to 2030/2031
findings.headline: Gross debt forecast to rise £1.0bn to £2.4bn, with prudential margins declining 21%
findings.detail: Gross debt (loans plus long-term liabilities) is forecast to increase from £1,395.8m at 31 March 2026 to £2,423.7m by 31 March 2031. Prudential margins—the buffer between gross debt and the capital financing requirement—are declining from £293.8m to £231.5m over the same period, leaving less headroom against the prudential limit.
findings.matters: Falling prudential margins indicate the council is utilising its borrowing headroom more aggressively. While margins remain healthy, this leaves less flexibility to respond to cost inflation, lower-than-forecast grant income, or increased capital needs.
findings.figures: Gross debt £1,395.8m to £2,423.7m (+73%); prudential margins £293.8m to £231.5m (-21%); margin still allows borrowing up to £2,655.3m CFR

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/2027 Treasury Management and Prudential Indicators 2026/2027 to 2030/2031
findings.headline: General fund financing costs rising to 8.34% of revenue by 2031, doubling from recent levels
findings.detail: General Fund loan charges (excluding PPP/leases) are forecast to rise from £46.5m (5.40% of revenue) in 2026/27 to £84.5m (8.34%) by 2030/31. When PPP/lease financing is included, total capital financing costs reach £98.2m (8.34% of £1,176.7m revenue budget).
findings.matters: Financing costs rising to 8% of revenue, while within prudent limits, reduces discretionary spending and resilience. The trajectory shows these costs will continue rising beyond 2031 as the capital programme is delivered and debt matures.
findings.figures: GF loan charges £46.5m rising to £84.5m; total GF financing costs £62.0m to £98.2m; financing costs as % of revenue 5.40% to 8.34%
findings.quote: Total General Fund : Capital Financing Costs 62. 0 70.4 82.6 95.0 98.2; General Fund : Net Revenue Stream 1,149.2 1,158.4 1,164.7 1,169.4 1,176.7; 5.40% 6.08% 7.10% 8.12% 8.34%

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/2027 Treasury Management and Prudential Indicators 2026/2027 to 2030/2031
findings.headline: HRA financing costs will consume 35% of housing revenue by 2031, up from 25% now
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account capital financing costs are rising dramatically from £45.9m (24.87% of HRA revenue) in 2026/27 to £79.3m (34.95%) by 2030/31. This means more than one-third of housing revenue will be consumed by debt servicing, constraining funds available for maintenance and management.
findings.matters: An HRA where financing costs exceed 30% of revenue signals unsustainable housing investment plans. Lenders assess HRA sustainability as a separate ring-fenced account, and rising financing ratios indicate either falling housing revenue or oversized capital programmes.
findings.figures: HRA financing costs rising from £45.9m (24.87% of revenue) to £79.3m (34.95% of revenue); HRA revenue forecast £184.6m to £226.9m

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/2027 Treasury Management and Prudential Indicators 2026/2027 to 2030/2031
findings.headline: Capital financing requirement increasing 57% to £2.7bn by 2031, driven by major capital programme
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to grow from £1,895.9m in 2026/27 to £2,655.3m by 2030/31, an increase of £765.4m over five years. This is driven by planned capital expenditure of £329.3m in 2026/27 (rising to £458.4m peak in 2028/29), with £236.3m funded by borrowing rather than grants or reserves.
findings.matters: A rapidly growing capital financing requirement indicates rising long-term debt servicing obligations. Lenders need to understand the sustainability of debt servicing from revenue, especially given the council's already constrained finances.
findings.quote: it is estimated that the Council will require to source long-term borrowing of £306.0m in 2026/2027, £312.0m in 2027/2028, £439.0m in 202 8/29, £196.0m in 20 29/30 and £175.5m in 2030/31

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Fraud investigation underway following concerns about potentially fraudulent business grant applications
findings.detail: Internal Audit undertook an investigation into potentially fraudulent applications for business grants by external parties. The investigation is ongoing, with the finalised report due for presentation to the Audit Panel in August 2026.
findings.matters: Active fraud investigation indicates control weaknesses in grant administration and potential financial loss from fraudulent claims.
findings.figures: One fraud investigation undertaken; findings to be reported in August 2026
findings.quote: One fraud investigation was undertaken during 2025-26. This followed concerns identified by officers in relation to potentially fraudulent applications for business grants by external parties. The investigation report is currently being finalised and will be presented at the next meeting of the Panel in August 2026 for discussion and consideration.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal Audit plan completion fell and coverage was reduced due to staffing constraints
findings.detail: The council operated with one vacant auditor post throughout most of 2025-26. Plan completion fell to 80.6% from 87.9% the prior year. Several planned audits were deferred or removed, including Project Management, Debt Management, and Compliance with Grant Conditions.
findings.matters: Reduced audit coverage and deferred work in areas like Debt Management mean less independent assurance over material governance and financial control areas.
findings.figures: Plan completion 80.6% vs 87.9% prior year; productive hours 85.9% vs 89.8%
findings.quote: The team experienced some staffing changes during 2025-26, which had the overall effect of operating with one vacant auditor post for much of the year. This resulted in some changes to the implementation of the audit plan.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Self-Directed Support audit identified significant control gaps around fund management and monitoring
findings.detail: The audit found significant weaknesses in applying procedures and retaining documentation across all four Self-Directed Support care delivery options, and inconsistency in monitoring Direct Payment expenditure. While no actual misuse was found in the sample tested, the weaknesses could allow funds to be misused, assessed needs to go unmet, and pose financial and reputational risk.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses in a service managing significant direct payments to service users present direct financial risk and expose the council to misuse of public funds.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinion affecting all four care delivery options
findings.quote: The audit found significant weaknesses in relation to the application of procedures and retention of key documentation for each of the four care delivery options available to service users, as well as in the consistency of monitoring Direct Payment expenditure. These weaknesses could lead to funds being misused, assessed needs not being met and potential financial loss and reputational damage for the Council (although there was no evidence of misuse of funds from the sample of cases tested).

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: School funds control weakness has persisted across multiple audit cycles without resolution
findings.detail: Audit testing at education establishments identified control weaknesses in school funds management, specifically non-compliance with procedures and insufficient oversight by Head teachers and senior management. This issue was mentioned in the 2024-25 audit report; previously agreed actions have still not been fully implemented. Further audit work is scheduled for 2026-27.
findings.matters: A control weakness persisting unresolved across consecutive audit cycles signals governance challenges and ineffective follow-up on audit recommendations.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinion in 2025-26; repeated audit activity over multiple years
findings.quote: The control environment around school funds has been subject of repeated audit activity over recent years and was mentioned specifically in the Internal Audit Annual Report for 2024-25. While work is ongoing to address the control weaknesses, the agreed actions from previous audits have not yet been fully implemented, meaning the areas of concern identified have not been addressed.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Asset Management Plan 2026-2031
findings.headline: Housing stock undergoing aggressive demolition of end-of-life properties
findings.detail: The council's Tower Strategy has identified numerous housing properties now beyond their operational lifecycle and is pursuing an aggressive demolition programme. This indicates substantial replacement capital need across the 36,880-home portfolio.
findings.matters: Large-scale demolition of end-of-life housing implies major forward capital requirements for replacement stock; indicates the housing asset base is aging and requires renewal.
findings.figures: 36,880 council homes; 1,240 additional homes added to valuation despite demolitions
findings.quote: Tower Strategy which has identified numerous properties that are now beyond their life cycle, and the mobilisation of an aggressive demolition programme.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Asset Management Plan 2026-2031
findings.headline: The Centre Cumbernauld acquired with deferred maintenance; scheduled demolition 2027–2031
findings.detail: North Lanarkshire acquired The Centre Cumbernauld shopping centre in June 2023 for town centre regeneration. The asset had received limited investment before acquisition and has required multiple essential repairs. Full demolition is planned over two stages concluding around 2031.
findings.matters: Acquisition of a distressed commercial asset requiring ongoing repairs and scheduled demolition within 4–8 years represents sunk capital cost and continuing maintenance burden; suggests council taking on deteriorating real estate.
findings.figures: Acquired June 2023; stage 1 closure ~2027, stage 2 closure ~2031
findings.quote: The asset had seen limited investment prior to North Lanarkshire Council's acquisition, which has resulted in a number of essential repairs over the last few years.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Asset Management Plan 2026-2031
findings.headline: Global inflation and material delays compounding capital project costs
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies that global inflation and ongoing local government financial pressure have created extremely challenging conditions. Construction material delays further compound rising costs for capital and maintenance works.
findings.matters: Rising capital costs reduce purchasing power of the £586.7m planned investment; supply delays risk slipping scheduled works into future years when costs may be higher.
findings.figures: £586.694m capital investment identified for 3-year period (2024-2029)
findings.quote: Global inflation, along with continued pressure on local government finances have created extremely challenging conditions within which we operate our assets. Economic conditions have resulted in increased costs for procuring capital and other works and this has been compounded with delays in the availability of construction materials.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Asset Management Plan 2026-2031
findings.headline: Non-domestic asset valuations declined £120m over five years despite active management
findings.detail: The council's non-domestic property portfolio, valued at £1.3bn, has fallen £0.12bn over five years. The plan attributes this to depreciation, disposals and portfolio adjustments, not market conditions alone.
findings.matters: Declining asset values reduce security available for borrowing and suggest the portfolio is aging faster than it is being renewed; contradicts typical council strategy.
findings.figures: £1.3bn current valuation; £0.12bn decline over 5 years
findings.quote: Over the last 5 years the value of the Council's non-domestic assets has decreased by £0.12bn.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Asset Management Plan 2026-2031
findings.headline: RAAC identified in multiple buildings; demolition chosen where remediation is uneconomical
findings.detail: The council's survey identified several buildings containing Reinforced Autoclaved Aerated Concrete (RAAC). Where remediation costs are prohibitive, demolition is being pursued. This has already resulted in closure of Motherwell Concert Hall and Civic Theatre.
findings.matters: RAAC remediation or demolition represents significant unplanned capital expenditure and service disruption; choosing demolition signals cost constraints limiting investment flexibility.
findings.figures: Motherwell Concert Hall and Civic Theatre confirmed closed; multiple unnamed buildings affected
findings.quote: Where remediation is not economically viable, and the cost of removal and reinstatement is prohibitive, demolition is being considered.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report 2026/27
findings.headline: The partnership faces a cumulative budget gap of £67.464m over three years, with medium-term and long-term financial sustainability rated 'Very High' risk.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget gap of £23.923m sits within a three-year Medium-Term Financial Plan gap of £67.464m (2026/27 to 2028/29). The partnership's own Risk Register rates both medium-term and long-term financial sustainability as 'Very High' risk. The strategic commissioning plan shows priorities (Prevention-Focused System, Tackling Inequality, etc.) but the paper gives no indication that these will reduce underlying demand or cost growth.
findings.matters: A 'Very High' risk rating on medium and long-term sustainability is a formal governance concern. For a lender, it signals that the partnership cannot currently articulate how it will close the £67.464m three-year gap without material service reduction, further savings, or external support.
findings.figures: £67.464m cumulative gap over three years; £23.923m gap in 2026/27
findings.quote: The plan highlighted a cumulative budget gap of £67.464m across the three-year period, including £23.923m in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Planned savings are only 59% delivered by end of Q1, with material gaps in social care and prescribing.
findings.detail: Of £23.923m planned savings for 2026/27, only £13.508m has been delivered by 30 June 2026. Prescribing review achieved £1.134m of a £4.416m target (gap £3.282m); Individual Budgets achieved £0.782m of £3.000m (gap £2.218m); Home First approach achieved £3.664m of £4.900m (gap £1.236m).
